offence_severity: Minimum: 6 months to maximum: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Fatal injuries resulting in coma and multiple skull fractures
number_of_offences: Charged under s.302 IPC; upheld under s.304 Part I IPC
premeditation_planning: Not found; the court found no evidence of reflection or planning
motive: Deceased's habitual abuse and threats towards the appellant
key_evidence_accepted: The fact that the appellant and the deceased were together the night when the deceased suffered the fatal injuries is established and proven. The chain of facts and circumstances established beyond doubt bars that the appellant and no other person was the perpetrator who had inflicted the injuries on his brother.
witness_credibility: The public witnesses, though declared hostile, have more or less in unison deposed that the appellant and the deceased used to stay in separate rooms at the same house. Their testimonies are important as they were present in the house at the time of the incident.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant had suffered from burn injuries in his hands, which he had accepted in his statement under Section 313 of the Cr.P.C. The appellant had tried to commit suicide by catching live electrical wires and was consequently sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for 10 days.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: Not stated
legal_representation: Harinder Mohan Singh, Adv. for the Appellant; Sumeer Sodhi, Dhruv Wadhwa, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under s.302 IPC; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Conviction converted to Part I of s.304 IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of his brother due to grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased had a history of abusing and threatening the appellant. The deceased had consumed alcohol and told the appellant to leave the house, otherwise he would kill him, leading to a sudden loss of self-control by the appellant.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant's actions were a result of grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased's abusive behavior over time led to a loss of self-control. The appellant had tried to commit suicide by holding live electrical wires, indicating a temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle of Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC, which recognizes that culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or another person by mistake or accident.
precedent_relied_upon: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra [1962] 1 Suppl. SCR 567; Budhi Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2012) 13 SCC 663 : [2012] 11 SCR 848; Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar [1966] 1 SCR 134
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed after considering that the appellant had already served over 10 years in custody, and the court modified the sentence to the period already undergone, with a fine of Rs. 1,000/- or simple imprisonment for six months in default.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the appellant's prior incarceration for over 10 years and the fact that the act was a result of grave and sudden provocation, leading to a temporary loss of self-control.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was directed to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/- and, in default, undergo simple imprisonment for six months. Upon payment of the fine or default imprisonment, the appellant was to be released forthwith.
